¶
'''behorn†''' (bē-hôrn′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''horn.''] To put horns on; cuckold.

'''behote†''', ''v.'' Same as ''behight.''

'''behourd''', ''n.'' [OF., also written ''behourt'', ''behour'', ''bihour'', ''bohourd'', etc., “a juste or tourney of many together with launces and batleaxes; also a bustling or blustering noise” (Cotgrave); < ''behourder'', ''behourdir'', “to just together with launces,” < ''behourt'', a lance.] A variety of the just practised in the thirteenth century, or, in some cases, a variety of the tourney.

'''behovable, behoveable''', ''a.'' See ''behoovable.''

'''behove''', ''v.'' Less correct spelling of ''behoove.''

'''behovely†''', ''a.'' [ME. (mod. as if *''behoofly''): see ''behoof'' and ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Necessary; advantageous. ''Chaucer.''

'''behowl''' (bē-houl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''howl.''] To howl at.
{{smaller block|The wolf ''behowls'' the moon.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 2.}}}}

'''behung''' (bē-hung′), ''p. a.'' [Pp. of *''behang'', not used, < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hang.''] Draped; ornamented with something hanging: as, a horse ''behung'' with trappings. [Rare.]

'''beid-el-sar''' (bād-el-sär′), ''n.'' [Ar.] A plant used in Africa as a remedy for various cutaneous affections. {{smaller|It is the ''Calotropis procera'', an asclepiadaceous shrub of tropical Africa and southern Asia. The Egyptians use the down of its seeds as tinder.}}

'''beige''' (bāzh), ''a.'' [F., < It. ''bigio'', gray: see ''bice.''] Having its natural color: said of a woolen fab-

readings.c3s2:
¶
'''beinness''' (bēn′nes), ''n.'' [Also spelled ''bienness'', < ''bein'', ''bien'', + ''-ness''.] Plenty; affluence; prosperousness; the state of being well off or well to do. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There was a prevailing air of comfort and ''bienness'' about the people and their houses.
{{right|''W. Black'', Princess of Thule, ii.}}}}

'''Beiram''', ''n.'' See ''Bairam''.

'''beistings''', ''n. sing.'' or ''pl.'' See ''beestings''.

'''beit''' (bēt), ''v. t.'' [Sc.] Same as ''beet''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bejade†''' (bē-jād′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jade''<sup>1</sup>.] To tire.
{{smaller block|Lest you ''bejade'' the good galloway.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

'''bejan''' (bē′ja̤n), ''n.'' [Sc., < F. ''béjaune'', < OF. ''becjaune'', a novice, lit. a yellow-beak, i. e., a young bird, < ''bec'', beak, + ''jaune'', yellow, a yellow beak being characteristic of young birds. See ''beak''<sup>1</sup> and ''jaundice''.] A student of the first or lowest class in the universities of St. Andrews and Aberdeen, Scotland.

'''bejape†''' (bē-jāp′), ''v. t.'' [ME.; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jape''.] '''1.''' To trick; deceive.
{{smaller block|Thou . . . hast ''byjaped'' here duk Theseus.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 727.}}}}
'''2.''' To laugh at; make a mock of.
{{smaller block|<poem>I shal ''byjaped'' ben a thousand tyme
More than that fool of whos folye men ryme.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 532.}}}}

'''bejaundice''' (bē-jän′dis), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jaundice''.] To infect with the jaundice.

'''bejesuit''' (bē-jez̮′ū-it), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''Jesuit''.] To infect or influence with Jesuitry.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|Who hath so ''bejesuited'' us that we should trouble that man with asking license to doe so worthy a deed?
{{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica, p. 54.}}}}

¶
'''bejewel''' (bē-jö′el), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jewel.''] To provide or adorn with jewels.
{{smaller block|Her ''bejewelled'' hands lay sprawling in her amber satin lap.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, I. xxi.}}}}

'''bejuco''' (Sp. pron. bā-hö′kō), ''n.'' [Sp.] A Spanish name for several species of the lianes or tall climbing plants of the tropics, such as ''Hippocratea scandens'', etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>The serpent-like ''bejuco'' winds his spiral fold on fold
Round the tall and stately ceiba till it withers in his hold.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Slaves of Martinique.}}}}

'''bejumble''' (bē-jum′bl), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jumble.''] To throw into confusion; jumble. ''Ash.''

'''bekah''' (bē′kä), ''n.'' [Heb.] An ancient Hebrew unit of weight, equal to half a shekel, 7.08 grams, or 109¼ grains. Ex. xxxviii. 26.

'''beken'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v. t.'' [ME. ''bekennen, bikennen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ken''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To make known.—'''2.''' To deliver.—'''3.''' To commit or commend to the care of.
{{smaller block|The devil I ''bykenne'' him.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Pardoner’s Tale, l. 6 (Harleian MS.).}}}}

'''beken'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.'' Same as ''behen.''

'''bekiss''' (bē-kis′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''kiss.''] To kiss repeatedly; cover with kisses. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|She’s sick of the young shepherd that ''bekissed'' her.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|beholding|510|bekiss}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Oh, I thank you, I am much ''beholding'' to you.
{{right|''Chapman'', Blind Beggar.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is in the power of every hand to destroy us, and we are ''beholding'' unto every one we meet, he doth not kill us.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, i. 44.}}}}

'''2.''' Attractive; fascinating.

{{smaller block|When he saw me, I assure you, my beauty was not more ''beholding'' to him than my harmony.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i. 50.}}}}

'''beholdingness''' (bē-hōl′ding-nes), ''n.'' The state of being beholden or under obligation to any one.

{{smaller block|Thank me, ye gods, with much ''beholdingnesse.'' For marke, I doe not curse you.
{{right|''Marston'', Sophonisba, v. 2.}}}}

'''behoney''' (bē-hun′i), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''honey.'']   To cover or smear with honey; sweeten with honey, or with honeyed words.

'''behoof''' (bē-höf′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''behōf'' (chiefly in the dat. ''behove'', with prep. ''to'', ''til'', or ''for''), < AS. *''behōf'', advantage (in deriv. ''behōflīc'', advantageous, ''behēfe'', useful, necessary, ''behōfian'', behoove: see ''behoove'') (= OFries. ''behōf'', ''bihōf'' = D. ''behoef'' = MLG. ''behōf'' = MHG. ''bihuof'', G. ''behuf'', advantage, = Sw. ''behof'' = Dan. ''behov'', need, necessity; cf. Icel. ''hōf'', moderation, measure, Goth. ''ga-hōbains'', self-restraint), < *''behebban'' (pret. *''behōf'') = MHG. ''beheben'', take, hold, < ''be-'' + ''hebban'', heave, raise, orig. take up, take: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''heave.'' In the phrase ''in'' or ''on behoof of'', the word is confused with ''behalf.'']   That which is advantageous to a person; behalf; interest; advantage; profit; benefit.

{{smaller block|Accordeth nought to the ''behove'' <poem>Of resonable mannes use.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i. 15.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>No mean recompense it brings
To your ''behoof''. ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 982.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who wants the finer politic sense
To mask, tho’ but in his own ''behoof'',
With a glassy smile his brutal scorn.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, vi.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Is not, indeed, every man a student, and do not all things exist for the student’s ''behoof?''
{{right|''Emerson'', Misc., p. 73.}}}}
{{smaller block|[This word is probably never used as a nominative, being regularly governed by one of the prepositions ''to'', ''for'', ''in'', or ''on'', and limited by a possessive word or phrase. ''Behalf'' is used similarly.]}}

'''behoofful†''', ''a.'' The more correct form of ''behooveful''.

'''behoovable''' (bē-hö′va̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''behoove'' + ''-able''.]   Useful; profitable; needful; fit. Also spelled ''behovable'' and ''behoveable''. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|All spiritual graces ''behoveable'' for our soul.
{{right|''Book of Homilies'', ii.}}}}

'''behoove''' (bē-höv′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''behooved'', ppr. ''behooving''.   [Also spelled, against analogy, ''behove''; < ME. ''behoven'', ''behofen'', AS. ''behōfian'', need, be necessary (= OFries. ''bihōvia'' = D. ''behoeven'' = MLG. ''behoven'', LG. ''behoben'', ''behöben'' = G. ''behufen'' (obs.) = Sw. ''behöfva'' = Dan. ''behöve''); from the noun: see ''behoof''. Cf. Icel. ''hæfa'', aim at, hit, behoove, = Sw. ''höfvas'', beseem. The pret. ''behooved'' is worn down in Sc. to ''bud'', ''bid'': see ''bid''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To be fit or meet for, with respect to necessity, duty, or convenience; be necessary for; become: now used only in the third person singular with ''it'' as subject.
{{smaller block|<poem>''It behoves'' the high,
For their own sakes, to do things worthily.</poem> {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Indeed, ''it behoved'' him to keep on good terms with his pupils. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book.}}}}

{{smaller block|He is sure of himself, and never needs to ask another what in any crisis ''it behooves'' him to do. {{right|''Emerson'', War.}}}}

'''2†.''' To relate to the advantage of; concern the well-being of: formerly used with a regular nominative.

<poem>If you know aught which does ''behove'' my knowledge
Thereof to be inform’d, imprison it not
In ignorant concealment.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2.}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To be necessary, suitable, or fit.

{{smaller block|Sometime ''behooveth'' it to be counselled. {{right|''Chaucer'', Melibeus.}}}}

{{smaller block|He had all those endowments mightily at command which are ''behoved'' in a scholar. {{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Life of Abp. Williams, I. 39.}}}}

Also spelled ''behove''.

'''behoove†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form (properly dative) of ''behoof.''

'''behooveful†''' (bē-höv′fu̇l), ''a.''   [Prop., as in early mod. E., ''behoofful'', < ME. ''behoveful'', < ''behof'', behoof, + ''-ful''.]   Needful; useful; fit; profitable; advantageous.

<poem>Madam, we have cull’d such necessaries
As are ''behoveful'' for our state to-morrow.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 3.}}

{{smaller block|It may be most ''behooveful'' for princes, in matters of grace, to transact the same publicly. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}

'''behoovefully†''' (bē-höv′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Usefully; profitably; necessarily.

'''behorn†''' (bē-hôrn′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''horn.'']   To put horns on; cuckold.

'''behote†''', ''v.'' Same as ''behight.''

'''behourd''', ''n.''   [OF., also written ''behourt'', ''behour'', ''bihour'', ''bohourd'', etc., “a juste or tourney of many together with launces and batleaxes; also a bustling or blustering noise” (Cotgrave); < ''behourder'', ''behourdir'', “to just together with launces,” < ''behourt'', a lance.]   A variety of the just practised in the thirteenth century, or, in some cases, a variety of the tourney.

'''behovable, behoveable''', ''a.'' See ''behoovable.''

'''behove''', ''v.'' Less correct spelling of ''behoove.''

'''behovely†''', ''a.''   [ME. (mod. as if *''behoofly''): see ''behoof'' and ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Necessary; advantageous.   ''Chaucer.''

'''behowl''' (bē-houl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''howl.'']   To howl at.
{{smaller block|The wolf ''behowls'' the moon.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 2.}}}}

'''behung''' (bē-hung′), ''p. a.''   [Pp. of *''behang'', not used, < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hang.'']   Draped; ornamented with something hanging: as, a horse ''behung'' with trappings. [Rare.]

'''beid-el-sar''' (bād-el-sär′), ''n.''   [Ar.]   A plant used in Africa as a remedy for various cutaneous affections. {{smaller|It is the ''Calotropis procera'', an asclepiadaceous shrub of tropical Africa and southern Asia. The Egyptians use the down of its seeds as tinder.}}

'''beige''' (bāzh), ''a.''   [F., < It. ''bigio'', gray: see ''bice.'']   Having its natural color: said of a woolen fabric made of undyed wool.

'''beild''', ''n.'' and ''v. t.'' See ''bield''.

'''beildy''', ''a.'' See ''bieldy''.

'''bein''' (bēn), ''a.''   [Also ''been'', ''bene'', Sc. also ''bien'', < ME. ''been'', ''beene'', ''bene''; origin unknown. The Icel. ''beinn'', hospitable, lit. straight, is a different word, the source of E. ''bain''<sup>1</sup>, ready, willing, etc.: see ''bain''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Wealthy; well to do: as, a ''bein'' farmer; a ''bein'' body.—'''2.''' Well provided; comfortable; cozy.
{{smaller block|This is a gey ''bein'' place, and it’s a comfort to hae sic a corner to sit in in a bad day. {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, II. xxiv.}}}}
[Now only Scotch.]

'''bein''' (bēn), ''adv.''   [Also ''bien''; < ''bein'', ''a.'']   Comfortably. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I grudge a wee the great folks’ gift,
That live sae ''bien'' and snug.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Ep. to Davie, i.}}}}

'''being''' (bē′ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''beynge'', ''byinge'', verbal n. of ''been'', be.]   '''1.''' Existence in its most comprehensive sense, as opposed to non-existence; existence, whether real or only in thought.—'''2.''' In ''metaph.'', subsistence in a state not necessarily amounting to actual existence; rudimentary existence. {{smaller|But the word is used in different senses by different philosophers. Hegel defines it as immediacy, that is, the abstract character of the present. In its most proper acceptation, it is the name given by philosophical reflection to that which is revealed in immediate consciousness independently of the distinction of subject and object. It may also be defined, but with less precision, as the abstract noun corresponding to the concrete class embracing every object. ''Being'' is also used in philosophy influenced by Aristotle to signify the rudiment or germ of existence, consisting in a nature, or principle of growth, before actual existence. It is also frequently used to mean actual existence, the complete preparation to produce effects on the senses and on other objects. Psychologically, ''being'' may be defined as the objectification of consciousness, though the distinction of subject from object logically presupposes being.}}
{{smaller block|Wee may well reject a Liturgie which had no ''being'' that wee can know of, but from the corruptest times.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
{{smaller block|First, Thou madest things which should have ''being'' without life. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, The Creation.}}}}
{{smaller block|Consider everything as not yet in ''being''; then consider if it must needs have been at all. {{right|''Bentley.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Our noisy years seem moments in the ''being''
Of the eternal Silence.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Ode to Immortality.}}}}

'''3.''' That which exists; anything that is: as, inanimate ''beings''.
{{smaller block|<poem>What a sweet ''being'' is an honest mind!</poem>
{{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, v. 1.}}}}

'''4.''' Life; conscious existence.
{{smaller block|I will sing praises unto my God while I have any ''being''.
{{right|Ps. cxlvi. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I fetch my life and ''being''
From men of royal siege.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I felt and feel, tho’ left alone,
His ''being'' working in mine own.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lxxxv.}}}}

'''5.''' Lifetime; mortal existence.
{{smaller block|<poem>Claudius, thou
Wast follower of his fortunes in his ''being''.</poem>
{{right|''Webster.''}}}}

{{smaller block|It is, as far as it relates to our present ''being'', the great end of education to raise ourselves above the vulgar.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 69.}}}}
'''6.''' That which has life; a living existence, in contradistinction to what is without life; a creature.

{{smaller block|It is folly to seek the approbation of any ''being'' besides the Supreme, because no other ''being'' can make a right judgment of us.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Accidental being,''' the being of an accident, mark, or quality.—'''Actual being,''' complete being; being really brought to pass; actuality.—'''Being in itself,''' being apart from the sentient consciousness; being per se.—'''Being of existence,''' historical being; existence.—'''Being per accidens,''' being through something extraneous.—'''Being per se,''' essential and necessary being.—'''Connotative being,''' a mode of being relative to something else.—'''Diminute being.''' See ''diminute''.—'''Intentional''' or '''spiritual being,''' the being of that which is in the mind.—'''Material being,''' what belongs to material bodies.—'''Natural being,''' that which belongs to things and persons.—'''Objective being,''' an expression formerly applied to the mode of being of an immediate object of thought, but in a modern writing it would be understood to mean the being of a real thing, existing independently of the mind. See ''objective''.—'''Potential being,''' that which belongs to something which satisfies the prerequisite conditions of existence, but is not yet complete or an actual fact.—'''Pure being,''' in ''metaph.'', the conception of being as such, that is, devoid of all predicates; being of which nothing can be affirmed except that it is.—'''Quidditative being,''' or '''being of essence,''' that being that belongs to things before they exist, in the bosom of the eternal.—'''Substantial being,''' the being of a substance.—'''To differ by the whole of being.''' See ''differ''.}}

'''being-place†''' (bē′ing-plās), ''n.'' A place to exist in; a state of existence.
{{smaller block|<poem>Before this worlds great frame, in which al things
Are now containd, found any ''being-place.''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Heavenly Love, l. 23.}}}}

'''beinly''' (bēn′li), ''adv.''   [< ''bein'' + ''-ly''.]   Comfortably; abundantly; happily; well. Also spelled ''bienly''. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|The children were likewise ''beinly'' apparelled.
{{right|''R. Gilhaize'', iii. 104.}}}}

'''beinness''' (bēn′nes), ''n.''   [Also spelled ''bienness'', < ''bein'', ''bien'', + ''-ness''.]   Plenty; affluence; prosperousness; the state of being well off or well to do. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There was a prevailing air of comfort and ''bienness'' about the people and their houses.
{{right|''W. Black'', Princess of Thule, ii.}}}}

'''Beiram''', ''n.'' See ''Bairam''.

'''beistings''', ''n. sing.'' or ''pl.'' See ''beestings''.

'''beit''' (bēt), ''v. t.''   [Sc.]   Same as ''beet''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bejade†''' (bē-jād′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jade''<sup>1</sup>.]   To tire.
{{smaller block|Lest you ''bejade'' the good galloway.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

''becjaune'', a novice, lit. a yellow-beak, i. e., a young bird, < ''bec'', beak, + ''jaune'', yellow, a yellow beak being characteristic of young birds. See ''beak''<sup>1</sup> and ''jaundice''.]   A student of the first or lowest class in the universities of St. Andrews and Aberdeen, Scotland.

{{smaller block|Thou . . . hast ''byjaped'' here duk Theseus.

{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 532.}}}}

'''bejesuit''' (bē-jez̮′ū-it), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''Jesuit''.]   To infect or influence with Jesuitry. {{smaller block|Who hath so ''bejesuited'' us that we should trouble that man with asking license to doe so worthy a deed?
{{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica, p. 54.}}}}

'''bejewel''' (bē-jö′el), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''jewel.'']   To provide or adorn with jewels.
{{smaller block|Her ''bejewelled'' hands lay sprawling in her amber satin lap.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, I. xxi.}}}}

'''bekah''' (bē′kä), ''n.''   [Heb.]   An ancient Hebrew unit of weight, equal to half a shekel, 7.08 grams, or 109¼ grains. Ex. xxxviii. 26.

'''beken'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v. t.''   [ME. ''bekennen, bikennen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ken''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To make known.—'''2.''' To deliver.—'''3.''' To commit or commend to the care of.
